standard.title: Investigable Questions, Predictions and Hypotheses
standard.description: develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to test relationships and develop explanatory models
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can develop questions, make predictions and formulate methods to investigate (AC9S7I01). They have not yet developed formal hypotheses specifying a testable relationship (if-then-because structure) or developed questions targeted at testing a relationship or building an explanatory model rather than simply exploring a phenomenon.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop investigable questions that target a specific relationship between variables, write reasoned predictions, and formulate hypotheses that can be supported or refuted through evidence — in contexts requiring explanation of body systems, energy transfer or chemical reactions. Students can develop questions intended to explore an explanatory model and explain what would constitute supporting or refuting evidence.

nodes.label: What makes a question investigable?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions, and explain the criteria that make a scientific question investigable — including that it must be answerable through observable, measurable evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether two contrasting questions are investigable or not, and explain what makes the investigable one testable (names variables, answerable by measurement or observation).
nodes.typical_width: Describe the criteria for an investigable question (observable/measurable variables, specific enough to test, not answered by opinion alone) and apply these criteria to evaluate and improve sample questions.
wider: Distinguish investigable questions from those that are philosophical, ethical or definitional — building precision about the scope of empirical investigation.
Examine how investigable questions arise from existing models — connecting the 'why does this happen?' question to an existing theoretical explanation that generates testable predictions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify what makes a question investigable will produce unfocused investigation designs at the next capability stage (AC9S9I02). A question that is too vague, not measurable, or not about a testable relationship cannot lead to a valid investigation method — the question quality determines the investigation quality.

response_modes.reason: The criteria for investigability are not self-evident. Students need the explicit reasoning: 'To be investigable, a question must name (or imply) variables that can be measured or observed. It must be answerable by data, not opinion. And it must be specific enough that one investigation could address it.' Model this evaluation with contrasting examples.

success_criteria: Can identify whether a question is investigable and explain why or why not.
Can improve a vague question by making it specific about variables.
Does not treat 'interesting' as a criterion for investigability — uses testability.

nodes.label: Reasoned predictions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write a reasoned prediction that states an expected outcome and provides a reason based on scientific knowledge — not just a guess.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a prediction for one scenario that includes an expected outcome and a reason grounded in scientific knowledge (e.g. 'I predict that increasing light intensity will increase the rate of photosynthesis because more light energy is available for the process').
nodes.typical_width: Write reasoned predictions for two or three investigable questions across different content domains, ensuring each prediction includes an expected outcome AND a scientific reason — distinguishing these from guesses or intuitions.
wider: Examine predictions that conflict with intuition — cases where scientific knowledge predicts an unexpected outcome — to build appreciation that scientific prediction differs from common sense.

Develop predictions for questions about relationships between human body systems (e.g. 'How does exercise intensity affect heart rate and breathing rate?') — connecting prediction-writing to the Y9 content.

response_modes.reason: Students routinely drop the reasoning component from predictions, treating them as guesses rather than evidence-based claims. Consistent practice with the expected-outcome + reason format — and correction when the reason is absent or not scientific — builds the habit before hypothesis writing.

success_criteria: Can write a prediction that includes both an expected outcome and a scientific reason.
Can distinguish a reasoned prediction from a guess — the reason is grounded in science, not preference.
Does not omit the reason — treats the because-clause as mandatory.

nodes.label: Hypotheses: testable, refutable, relationship-specifying
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write a formal hypothesis that specifies the predicted relationship between variables in a form that can be supported or refuted through evidence, and explain why scientific hypotheses must be refutable.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a hypothesis for one investigation using an if-then-because structure (or equivalent), specifying the independent variable, predicted effect on dependent variable, and a reason. Explain why the hypothesis must be refutable — what result would refute it.
nodes.typical_width: Write hypotheses for two or three investigations and evaluate each for refutability — identifying what evidence would support it and what evidence would refute it. Explain why a hypothesis that cannot be refuted is not scientifically useful.
wider: Examine the concept of a null hypothesis — the prediction that there is no effect — and explain how it is used alongside the experimental hypothesis in formal scientific investigations.

Develop hypotheses to explore an explanatory model (e.g. 'If heat energy transfers from higher to lower temperature until equilibrium is reached, then placing objects of different temperatures in contact will result in...') — connecting hypothesis writing to model testing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who write unfalsifiable hypotheses (e.g. 'plants will grow differently') cannot use investigation results to either support or refute their hypothesis — the conclusion stage of the investigation collapses. Refutability is the hinge: a hypothesis that cannot be tested cannot be advanced or rejected, and the entire investigation loses its logical structure.

response_modes.reason: The concept of refutability is philosophically non-trivial. Scaffold the argument: 'If no possible result could prove your hypothesis wrong, then your hypothesis doesn't actually predict anything testable — it's not a scientific hypothesis.' Concrete counter-examples (e.g. 'plants respond to their environment' — true but untestable) make this clearer than abstract explanation.

success_criteria: Can write a hypothesis that specifies the relationship between named variables.
Can identify what result would refute their hypothesis.
Does not write vague or circular hypotheses — the prediction must be specific enough to test.
